t: Minimum Moves to Balance Circular Array
o: One person may hold a negative balance (guaranteed at most one). Each move shifts 1 unit between neighbors on a ring; minimize total moves so everyone is ≥ 0. If the total sum is negative it is impossible (-1); if nobody is negative the answer is 0. For [5,1,-4] the deficit 4 is filled with 1 unit from the neighbor at distance 1 and 3 units from the node at distance 1 the other way: 4 moves. For [1,2,-5,2] the answer is 6.
k: Feasibility depends only on the total sum being non-negative.
Each delivered unit travels its shortest circular path independently; greedily consume surplus from nearest nodes first.

a.i: Units passing through intermediate nodes cause no issue (a node receives then forwards, staying non-negative), so each of the d needed units can be routed along its shortest arc independently. Total cost is minimized by taking surplus in increasing order of circular distance to the deficient node — a classical transportation problem with linear costs and independent demands.
s: If sum(balance) < 0 return -1; if no negatives return 0.
Locate the negative node p with need = -balance[p].
For every other node compute dist = min(clockwise, counterclockwise) distance to p, paired with its surplus amount; sort by distance.
Take min(surplus, remaining need) units from each node in order, adding take*dist to the answer, until the need is met.
a.t: O(n log n) — dominated by sorting surplus nodes by distance

w: Justify the greedy: edge traversals decompose per unit, and no capacity constraints exist on edges, so the multiset of unit-paths is independent — nearest-first is optimal. Watch 64-bit arithmetic (need up to 1e9 times distance up to 1e5/2). Pitfall: treating the ring as linear and missing the wrap-around direction. Follow-up: multiple negative nodes (then it becomes a min-cost flow / classic gas-station-style redistribution), or directed transfers.
